# 7. Business Role Permission Assignment

Permissions must be assigned to Groups.

For example:

```text
Group: Manager

Client Roles:
    orders.read
    orders.update
    stores.read
    stores.manage
```

A user assigned to the `Manager` Group inherits those role mappings through Keycloak.

Do not assign normal business permissions directly to every user unless there is an explicit exceptional requirement.

The preferred model is:

```text
User
    -> Group
        -> Client Roles
```

rather than:

```text
User
    -> hundreds of directly assigned roles
```

---

Create or identify a protected system administrator Group.

For example:

```text
/Admin
```

or:

```text
/SystemAdministrators
```

The exact name should follow existing conventions.

The default/bootstrap administrator must be a member of this Group.

The Group represents the application's privileged administrative business role.

Do NOT duplicate this relationship in Oracle.

---

# 9. New Permissions Must Automatically Be Assigned to Admin

Whenever a service registers a new permission, the System Administrator Group must automatically receive that permission.

Example:

Before deployment:

```text

orders.update
```

After a new service version starts:

```text
orders.read
orders.update
orders.export
orders.cancel
```

Registration must result in:

```text
Admin Group
    -> orders.read
    -> orders.update
    -> orders.export
    -> orders.cancel
```

No manual Keycloak administration must be required.

The registration pipeline must perform this mapping automatically.

---

# 10. Permission Registration Flow

Services must be able to register their permissions through Identity Service.

Conceptually:

```text
Orders Service
       |
       | register permissions
       v
Identity Service
       |
       | validate / normalize / reconcile
       v

       |

       |
       +--> update metadata where applicable
       |
       +--> assign new permissions to Admin Group
```

Registration must be idempotent.

Calling it multiple times must not create duplicate roles.

Inspect existing service registration mechanisms.

If appropriate, expose something conceptually similar to:

```json
{
  "service": "orders-service",
  "permissions": [
    {
      "name": "orders.read",
      "description": "Read orders"

    {

      "description": "Create orders"

    {

      "description": "Cancel orders"
    }

```

```text
1. Resolve the correct Keycloak client.
2. Create missing client roles.
3. Reuse existing roles.
4. Reconcile appropriate metadata.
5. Automatically map required new roles to the Admin Group.
6. Return the normalized registered permission model.
```

Do not persist a second permission registry in Oracle.

Keycloak itself is the registry.

---

# 12. Permission Removal / Deprecation

Do not blindly delete a Keycloak Role simply because it is missing from one registration request.

A missing role may still be assigned to Groups or Users.

Design an explicit lifecycle strategy.

For example:

```text
register
update metadata
deprecate
disable logically if supported by application conventions
remove explicitly
```

Actual destructive removal must be deliberate.

Document the selected behavior.

---

# 13. Composite Roles

Inspect whether Composite Roles improve the existing architecture.

Keycloak Composite Roles may be useful for reusable permission bundles.

For example:

```text
orders.manager
    composite:
        orders.read
        orders.create
        orders.update
        orders.cancel
```

However, do not replace Business Role Groups with composite roles automatically.

The intended conceptual separation is:

```text
Group
    = Business Role / user collection

Client Role
    = Permission

Composite Role
    = optional reusable permission bundle
```

Use Composite Roles only when they simplify the actual project.

---

# 14. Default Administrator Membership

Bootstrap behavior must ensure that the intended default administrator user belongs to the Administrator Group.

This should be idempotent.

Do not rely on repeated manual configuration in the Keycloak Admin Console.

If Keycloak Default Groups are appropriate for a particular bootstrap flow, evaluate them.

However, be careful:

A generic Default Group is assigned to newly created users.

Therefore, the System Administrator Group must NOT accidentally become a default group for every newly created user.

The bootstrap administrator membership should be explicit and safe.

---

# 15. Dynamic Data Scopes

The application's concept of Scope is primarily a DATA AUTHORIZATION concept.

For example:

```json
{
  "region": ["tehran-1", "tehran-2"],
  "store": ["1", "2", "3"],
  "warehouse": ["10", "11"],
  "test-key": ["items-1"]
}
```

These values define which subset of application data a user may access.

Do not confuse this with:

```text
OAuth scope
OIDC client scope
Keycloak Authorization Services resource scope
```

Those are separate concepts.

Internally, use a clear name such as:

```text
DataScope
AccessScope
AuthorizationScope
```

where needed to avoid ambiguity.

The public API may continue using `scopes` if that contract is already established.

---

# 16. Dynamic Scope Requirement

Scope keys must remain completely dynamic.

Today:

```text
region
branch
store
```

Tomorrow:

```text
warehouse
sales-channel
department
customer-segment
test-key
custom-scope-x
```

Adding a new scope key must NOT require modifying C# DTO properties.

This design is forbidden:

```csharp
public List<string> Region { get; set; }
public List<string> Branch { get; set; }
public List<string> Store { get; set; }
public List<string> Warehouse { get; set; }
```

Use a generic representation such as:

```csharp
IReadOnlyDictionary<string, IReadOnlyCollection<string>>
```

for the normalized application model.

---

# 17. Correct Existing Scope Deserialization Problem

The existing failure involving:

```text
$.assignments[0].scopes.test-key
```

must be fixed.

Internally use a consistent representation.

For example:

```json
{
  "scopes": {
    "region": [
      "tehran-1",
      "tehran-2"
    ],
    "store": [
      "1",
      "2",
      "3"
    ],
    "test-key": [
      "items-1"
    ]
  }
}
```

Prefer arrays consistently.

If backward compatibility requires accepting:

```json
"test-key": "items-1"
```

implement a safe converter that normalizes it into:

```json
"test-key": ["items-1"]
```

Do not use:

```csharp
Dictionary<string, object>
```

as a shortcut.

---

# 18. Store Data Scopes in Keycloak Attributes

Scope data must be persisted in Keycloak.

Do not create Oracle Scope tables.

Use Keycloak custom attributes.

There are two different cases.

## Group-level scopes

Shared values that apply to all users of a Business Role may be Group Attributes.

Example:

```text
Group:
/RegionalManager

Attributes:

scope.allowed-types = region,store
```

or shared values where appropriate.

## User-specific scopes

Values that differ for individual users must normally be User Attributes.

Example:

Alice:

```text
region:
    tehran-1
    tehran-2

store:
    1
    2
    3
```

Bob:

```text
region:
    shiraz-1

store:
    8
```

Do not put user-specific values on the Group if doing so would make every Group member inherit the same values.

---

# 19. Establish a Stable Attribute Namespace

Do not store arbitrary authorization attributes without a naming convention.

Use a reserved namespace such as:

```text
authz.scope.region
authz.scope.store
authz.scope.warehouse
authz.scope.test-key
```

Example:

```text
authz.scope.store = ["1", "2", "3"]
authz.scope.region = ["tehran-1", "tehran-2"]
```

The exact naming convention may be improved after inspecting the existing project.

However:

```text
authz.scope.*
```

must be clearly distinguishable from unrelated profile attributes such as:

```text
phone
locale
employeeNumber
```

---

# 20. Alternative Structured Scope Attribute

Also evaluate whether one structured Keycloak attribute is more appropriate:

```text
authz.scopes
```

with conceptual content:

```json
{
  "region": [
    "tehran-1",
    "tehran-2"
  ],
  "store": [
    "1",
    "2",
    "3"
  ],
  "test-key": [
    "items-1"
  ]
}
```

Compare this against the prefixed multivalued-attribute design.

Select the design that works most reliably with:

```text
Keycloak Admin API
User Profile
Group Attributes
Protocol Mappers
Token generation
UserInfo
Introspection
future scope extension
```

Document the decision.

Do not add a database simply to avoid this design decision.

---

# 21. Prefer Multivalued Scope Semantics

The normalized application model should treat scope values as collections.

For example:

```text
store -> ["1", "2", "3"]
```

not:

```text
store -> "1,2,3"
```

Avoid delimiter-based serialization where Keycloak can represent multiple attribute values appropriately.

The Identity Service should normalize Keycloak's representation to:

```csharp
Dictionary<string, IReadOnlyCollection<string>>
```

or an equivalent immutable model.

---

# 22. Group Attributes and User Attributes

Keycloak supports both Group Attributes and User Attributes.

Design explicit merge semantics.

For example:

```text
Group scopes
    +
User scopes
    =
Effective scopes
```

Possible semantics may be:

```text
union
user override
intersection
```

Do NOT leave this undefined.

For authorization, overly permissive union semantics can broaden access unexpectedly.

Choose semantics based on the project's intended behavior.

At minimum distinguish:

```text
allowed scope types
default scope values
user-specific scope values
effective scope values
```

---

# 23. Recommended Scope Responsibility Model

Prefer separating configuration from assignment.

For example:

```text
Group: RegionalManager

Group attributes:
    authz.allowed-scopes = ["region", "store"]
```

User Alice:

```text
authz.scope.region = ["tehran-1", "tehran-2"]
authz.scope.store  = ["1", "2", "3"]
```

Meaning:

```text
RegionalManager may use:
    region
    store

Alice's actual values:
    region = tehran-1, tehran-2
    store  = 1, 2, 3
```

This allows the Admin UI to know which scope dimensions are valid for a Business Role without hardcoding them.

Evaluate this model against the current requirements.

---

# 24. Dynamic Scope Definitions

The Admin UI needs to know which scope keys can be selected.

Because Keycloak remains the source of truth, scope definitions should also be represented in Keycloak configuration rather than an Oracle ScopeDefinition table.

Evaluate safe representations such as:

```text
dedicated configuration Group
realm attributes/configuration where appropriate
group metadata
client attributes
managed user-profile metadata
```

or another native Keycloak-backed strategy.

Do not introduce Oracle solely to register scope keys.

The Identity Service must expose a normalized API:

```text
GET available data scopes
```

without requiring the frontend to know how they are physically represented in Keycloak.

---

# 25. Scope Ownership by Services

Services may declare supported scope types during registration.

For example:

```json
{
  "service": "orders-service",
  "permissions": [
    "orders.read",
    "orders.update"
  ],
  "scopes": [
    "region",
    "store"
  ]
}
```

Identity Service should reconcile this information with Keycloak.

A newly introduced scope definition such as:

```text
warehouse
```

must become available to administrative APIs without adding DTO properties or Oracle columns.

---

# 26. Resource-Specific Scope Metadata

A scope must not automatically be valid against every resource.

For example:

```text
store
    -> Orders
    -> Inventory

region
    -> Orders
    -> Stores

warehouse
    -> Inventory
```

This configuration should remain controlled.

If the service-registration contract already contains resource metadata, it may declare:

```json
{
  "resource": "orders",
  "supportedScopes": [
    "region",
    "store"
  ]
}
```

Persist the authoritative registration metadata in Keycloak configuration if persistence is necessary.

Do not allow arbitrary table names, SQL, property paths, or expressions to be registered from untrusted clients.

---

# 27. Scope Filtering Is Still Application Responsibility

Keycloak stores authorization identity and scope values.

Keycloak does NOT need to understand the application's EF Core database schema.

Example:

Keycloak provides:

```json
{
  "permissions": [
    "orders.read"
  ],
  "scopes": {
    "store": [
      "1",
      "2",
      "3"
    ]
  }
}
```

The Orders service may safely translate that into:

```csharp
query.Where(x => storeIds.Contains(x.StoreId))
```

The executable database mapping remains trusted application code.

Do not store arbitrary SQL or LINQ expressions in Keycloak attributes.

---

# 28. Token Claims

Create or configure appropriate Protocol Mappers so that applications receive normalized authorization context where useful.

Desired conceptual token/context:

```json
{
  "sub": "...",
  "preferred_username": "alice",

  "business_roles": [
    "Manager"
  ],

  "permissions": [
    "orders.read",
    "orders.update",
    "stores.read"
  ],

  "scopes": {
    "region": [
      "tehran-1",
      "tehran-2"
    ],
    "store": [
      "1",
      "2",
      "3"
    ]
  }
}
```

Do not assume the built-in mapper can automatically transform every dynamic attribute naming convention into the exact nested JSON structure.

First inspect what existing Protocol Mappers can do.

If necessary, implement a controlled custom Keycloak Protocol Mapper SPI that:

```text
reads authz.scope.* attributes
reads inherited Group attributes where appropriate
normalizes them
emits one structured "scopes" claim
```

Avoid custom Keycloak extensions if the standard mappers can cleanly satisfy the requirement.

---

# 29. Group Membership Claim

The application may need Business Role information.

Configure an appropriate Group Membership mapper if needed.

Do not unnecessarily expose internal Keycloak group hierarchy if the application only requires normalized Business Role names.

Identity Service may map:

```text
/groups/business/Manager
```

to:

```json
{
  "businessRole": "Manager"
}
```

if that fits the current API contract.

---

# 30. Effective Permissions

The normalized model returned by Identity Service should expose effective permissions.

Effective permissions include permissions inherited through Group role mappings and Composite Roles where applicable.

Do not only return directly assigned user roles.

The caller generally needs:

```text
effective permissions
```

not:

```text
only direct role mappings
```

---

# 31. Existing Sessions and Permission Changes

This requirement must be handled correctly.

Changing Group membership, roles, or user/group attributes in Keycloak does NOT rewrite an access token that has already been issued.

Therefore distinguish:

```text
Keycloak authorization state
```

from:

```text
claims inside an already-issued JWT
```

Do not claim otherwise.

A user should not need to manually logout/login whenever authorization changes.

Use one or more appropriate strategies:

```text
short-lived access tokens
refresh tokens
silent token refresh
token renewal
Keycloak introspection where appropriate
authorization request where appropriate
```

Choose based on the current application architecture.

---

# 32. No Manual Re-Login Requirement

The application UX requirement is:

```text
authorization changes should not require manual logout/login
```

This does NOT mean an old immutable JWT can magically change.

Instead:

```text
existing SSO session remains valid
        |
        v
access token can be refreshed
        |
        v
new claims reflect current Keycloak state
```

Configure token lifetime and refresh behavior accordingly.

Document the expected propagation delay.

---

# 33. Do Not Introduce a Local Authorization Database to Solve Token Freshness

Token freshness must NOT be solved by moving authorization to Oracle.

Keycloak remains authoritative.

If faster propagation or reduced Keycloak traffic is required later, the Identity Service may use Redis caching.

Redis would be a cache, not a source of truth.

Conceptually:

```text
Keycloak
    = source of truth

Redis
    = optional cache

Identity Service
    = wrapper/orchestrator/normalizer
```

---

# 34. Future Redis Support

Design interfaces so Redis can be introduced without changing public APIs.

For example:

```csharp
IIdentityProvider
IKeycloakAdminClient
IBusinessRoleStore
IPermissionStore
IScopeStore
IEffectiveAuthorizationReader
```

may be backed initially by Keycloak.

Later:

```text
read-through Redis cache
        |
        v
Keycloak
```

can be added.

Do NOT implement Redis unless required by the current task.

Do not make the architecture dependent on Redis.

---

# 35. Identity Service Responsibilities

Identity Service should own orchestration, not authorization persistence.

Expected responsibilities include:

```text
User management API
Group / Business Role management API
Permission registration API
Role mapping APIs
Scope management API
Keycloak model normalization
validation
service registration orchestration
token/model mapping
future caching
Vault/key orchestration
```

Identity Service should hide Keycloak-specific payload complexity from business applications.

---

# 36. User Management

User creation/update/delete/list operations must use Keycloak.

The Identity Service can continue exposing a clean domain-specific request such as:

```json
{
  "username": "alice",
  "email": "alice@example.com",
  "firstName": "Alice",
  "lastName": "Smith",
  "enabled": true
}
```

but persistence must remain in Keycloak.

Do not create an Oracle User table as a duplicate identity store.

---

# 37. Business Role Assignment

A request such as:

```json
{
  "userId": "...",
  "businessRole": "Manager"
}
```

must result in Keycloak Group membership.

Conceptually:

```text
User Alice
    joins
Group Manager
```

not:

```text
INSERT UserBusinessRole INTO Oracle
```

---

# 38. Full Assignment API

The external API may expose an application-friendly model such as:

```json
{
  "role": "Manager",
  "scopes": {
    "region": [
      "tehran-1",
      "tehran-2"
    ],
    "store": [
      "1",
      "2",
      "3"
    ],
    "test-key": [
      "items-1"
    ]
  }
}
```

Identity Service must translate this into Keycloak concepts:

```text
role
    -> Group membership

permissions
    -> inherited from Group role mappings

scope values
    -> appropriate user/group attributes
```

Do not mirror this object into an Oracle assignment table.

---

# 39. Multiple Business Roles

Users may belong to multiple Groups.

For example:

```text
Alice
    -> Manager
    -> Auditor
```

Define deterministic behavior for:

```text
effective permissions
effective scopes
duplicate permissions
duplicate scope values
conflicting scope configuration
```

Duplicate permissions should normally collapse naturally into a set.

Scope merging requires explicit semantics.

Test it.

---

# 40. Scope-to-Business-Role Validation

If a Group allows only:

```text
region
store
```

then this request:

```json
{
  "role": "RegionalManager",
  "scopes": {
    "warehouse": ["1"]
  }
}
```

must fail unless `warehouse` is allowed for that Group.

Do not accept every dynamic scope for every business role merely because the key exists.

Dynamic does not mean unrestricted.

---

# 41. Admin APIs

Identity Service should provide normalized APIs for at least:

```text
Users
Business Roles
Permissions
Group Permission Mappings
User Group Membership
Available Scope Definitions
Scope Values
Effective User Authorization
```

For example:

```text
GET /users/{id}

GET /business-roles

GET /business-roles/{id}

GET /business-roles/{id}/permissions

PUT /business-roles/{id}/permissions

GET /permissions

GET /scopes

GET /users/{id}/authorization
```

Adapt paths to existing project conventions.

Conceptually:

```json
{

    "Manager"

    "orders.read",

    ]
  }
}
```

Build this view from Keycloak.

Do not build it from duplicated Oracle authorization tables.

# 43. Keycloak Admin API Abstraction

Do not spread raw Keycloak Admin REST calls throughout controllers.

Introduce clear adapters/services.

For example:

```text
IKeycloakUserStore
IKeycloakGroupStore
IKeycloakRoleStore
IKeycloakScopeAttributeStore
IKeycloakClientStore
```

or use existing abstractions if the project already has suitable ones.

# 44. IBusinessRoleStore

Specifically inspect:

```csharp
IBusinessRoleStore
```

The intended implementation should now be approximately:

```text
IBusinessRoleStore
        |
        v
KeycloakBusinessRoleStore
        |
        v
Keycloak Group APIs
```

```text
CreateRole
GetRoles
AssignPermission
GetPermissions
```

map these concepts onto:

# 45. Oracle identity-meta-db Has a Limited Role

The `identity-meta-db` Oracle database should NOT store:

```text
users
groups/business roles
permissions
role mappings
user/group authorization assignments
dynamic scopes
scope values
```

when Keycloak already owns those concepts.

# 46. Appropriate Uses of identity-meta-db

Inspect the existing repository and use `identity-meta-db` only for Identity-Service-owned metadata that Keycloak should not own.

Current expected use includes metadata required for:

```text
cryptographic key orchestration
key rotation metadata
Keycloak key synchronization
Vault synchronization
integration state
technical synchronization checkpoints if required
```

```text
Vault key version
Keycloak imported key reference
rotation timestamp
synchronization status
```

that technical metadata may belong in Oracle.

Do not store raw secrets unnecessarily.

# 47. Vault Integration

Inspect current Vault integration.

The intended ownership is approximately:

```text
Vault
    -> secret/private key material where applicable

identity-meta-db
    -> technical metadata / synchronization state

Keycloak
    -> identity and authorization configuration
```

Do not place authorization data into Oracle merely because the database already exists.

---

# 48. Avoid Dual Writes

Avoid architecture such as:

```text
Create Group in Keycloak
+
Create BusinessRole row in Oracle
```

or:

```text
Create Role in Keycloak
+
Create Permission row in Oracle
```

or:

```text
Save scope attribute in Keycloak
+
Save AssignmentScope in Oracle
```

This creates distributed consistency problems with no clear benefit.

Unless a truly separate business requirement exists, use only Keycloak.

---

# 49. Keycloak User Profile

Inspect Keycloak User Profile configuration before introducing dynamic custom user attributes.

Ensure authorization-specific attributes can be managed by administrators without allowing normal users to grant themselves scopes.

This is a security-critical requirement.

A user must NOT be able to update:

```text
authz.scope.region
authz.scope.store
authz.scope.*
```

through self-service profile editing.

Only trusted administrative/service flows should be able to modify authorization attributes.

Configure attribute permissions accordingly.

---

# 50. Scope Security

Authorization scope attributes must be server-controlled.

A normal user must never be able to submit:

```json
{
  "authz.scope.store": [
    "1",
    "2",
    "3",
    "999"
  ]
}
```

through profile APIs and increase their own access.

Ensure:

```text
view/edit permissions
User Profile settings
Admin API permissions
Identity Service endpoint authorization
```

protect these attributes.

---

# 51. Admin Service Account

Identity Service will require appropriate credentials to manage Keycloak using Admin REST APIs.

Use a dedicated confidential client/service account with the minimum required Keycloak management privileges.

Do not use the human realm administrator credentials in application configuration.

Do not hardcode admin username/password.

Use existing secure secret management/Vault conventions.

---

# 52. Service Registration Authentication

A business service registering permissions must itself be authenticated and authorized.

Do not expose:

```text
POST /permissions/register
```

to arbitrary callers.

The service must be able to register only permissions within its permitted namespace/client.

For example:

```text
orders-service
```

must not be allowed to register:

```text
identity.admin.delete
```

unless explicitly authorized.

Validate service ownership.

---

# 53. Permission Namespace

Define a stable naming convention.

For example:

```text
{domain}.{resource}.{action}
```

Examples:

```text
orders.order.read
orders.order.create

inventory.item.read
inventory.item.update

identity.user.read
identity.user.manage
```

or retain the existing convention if already established.

Do not rename existing permissions without a migration strategy.

---

# 54. Admin Permission Synchronization

When permission registration creates a new Keycloak Role:

```text
1. Create/reuse role.
2. Resolve Admin Group.
3. Check whether role is already mapped.
4. Add missing Group role mapping.
```

This operation must be idempotent.

Also implement a reconciliation operation capable of repairing drift:

```text
all registered application permissions
    minus
Admin Group effective permissions
```

and assigning missing mappings.

This protects against partial failures or manual Keycloak modifications.

---

# 55. No Native Wildcard Assumption for Admin

Do NOT implement Admin as:

```text
role = "*"
```

or:

```text
mng.*.*
```

unless the application itself explicitly interprets it.

Prefer actual Keycloak mappings.

The registration/reconciliation process should make sure the Admin Group has all registered roles.

If a Composite Admin Role provides a cleaner implementation, evaluate:

```text
platform-admin
```

as a Composite Role containing all application permission roles.

Then:

```text
Admin Group
    -> platform-admin
```

and new permission registration adds the role to the composite.

This is a valid alternative.

Compare:

```text
A. Map all roles directly to Admin Group

B. platform-admin Composite Role
      contains all roles
   Admin Group
      receives platform-admin
```

Select the cleaner design based on the current realm/client structure.

---

# 56. Important Role/Group Separation

Maintain this conceptual distinction:

```text
Keycloak Group
    = Business Role / collection of users

Keycloak Client Role
    = atomic application permission

Keycloak Composite Role
    = optional permission bundle

Keycloak User/Group Attribute
    = dynamic data authorization scope
```

Do not collapse all four concepts into one abstraction.

---

# 57. Keycloak Authorization Services

Inspect whether Keycloak Authorization Services is already used.

Do not automatically introduce it if normal Client Roles + Groups + Attributes solve the requirements.

Keycloak Authorization Services provides:

```text
resources
authorization scopes
policies
permissions
UMA/RPT
```

and can be useful for fine-grained centralized resource authorization.

However, the current application's dynamic data filters such as:

```text
store = [1,2,3]
region = [tehran-1]
```

do not automatically become EF Core row filters just because Authorization Services exists.

Only use Authorization Services where it provides a clear benefit.

Avoid unnecessary complexity.

# 58. Token Size

Be aware that users may eventually have:

```text
many roles
many groups
many scope values
```

Do not blindly place unlimited authorization data in the Access Token.

Assess expected token size.

Consider exposing:

```text
business roles
effective permissions
essential scopes
```

according to application needs.

If scope values can become very large, evaluate whether they should instead be obtained from:

```text
UserInfo
Introspection
Identity Service authorization-context endpoint
```

while Keycloak remains the source of truth.

Document the tradeoff.

Create a normalized model independent of raw Keycloak JSON.

or an equivalent appropriate model.

```text
realm_access
resource_access
Keycloak GroupRepresentation
Keycloak UserRepresentation
raw attribute dictionaries
```

# 61. Admin UI Workflow

The intended administration workflow is:

```text
1. Admin UI requests Business Roles from Identity Service.

2. Identity Service reads Keycloak Groups.

3. Admin selects Manager.

4. Admin UI requests available Permissions.

5. Identity Service reads Keycloak Client Roles.

6. Admin maps permissions to Manager.

7. Identity Service updates Group Role Mappings in Keycloak.

8. Admin selects allowed Data Scope definitions.

9. Admin assigns dynamic values such as:
       store = [1,2,3]

10. Identity Service writes the appropriate Keycloak attributes.

11. User authorization context reflects those Keycloak values.
```

# 62. Service Registration Example

Example service registration:

```json
{
  "service": "inventory-service",

  "permissions": [
    "inventory.item.read",
    "inventory.item.update",
    "inventory.warehouse.read"
  ],

  "scopes": [
    "warehouse",
    "store"
  ]
}
```

Expected behavior:

```text
Identity Service
    |
    +--> ensure Keycloak client exists / resolve configured client
    |
    +--> ensure client roles exist
    |
    +--> register/reconcile scope metadata in Keycloak
    |
    +--> automatically grant new permission roles to Admin Group
```

No Oracle Permission or Scope rows should be created.

---

# 63. User Creation Example

This request:

```json
{
  "username": "alice",
  "email": "alice@example.com",
  "firstName": "Alice",
  "lastName": "Smith",
  "enabled": true,

  "assignments": [
    {
      "role": "Manager",
      "scopes": {
        "region": [
          "tehran-1",
          "tehran-2"
        ],
        "store": [
          "1",
          "2",
          "3"
        ],
        "test-key": [
          "items-1"
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

must result in:

```text
Create/update Alice in Keycloak

Join Alice to Manager Group

Validate Manager supports:
    region
    store
    test-key

Persist scope values using the chosen Keycloak attribute representation
```

No C# `TestKey` property is allowed.

No Oracle `AssignmentScope` row is allowed.

---

# 64. Scope Validation Providers

Scope keys can be dynamic, but some values may need validation against business services.

Example:

```text
store = [1,2,3]
```

may require validation against Store Service.

Identity Service may use a provider abstraction:

```csharp
IScopeValueProvider
```

for retrieving selectable values.

For example:

```text
store
    -> Store Service

region
    -> Region Service
```

This provider registry is executable application configuration, not arbitrary user input.

Do not allow clients to supply arbitrary service URLs or SQL.

---

# 65. Scope Value Persistence Still Belongs to Keycloak

Even when values are discovered from another service:

```text
Store Service
    -> available values 1,2,3,4
```

and Admin assigns:

```text
1,2,3
```

the authorization assignment itself must be stored in Keycloak attributes.

Do not copy the assignment into Oracle.

---

# 66. identity-meta-db Refactoring

Inspect all current usages of:

```text
identity-meta-db
```

Classify each table/data model into:

```text
A. Authorization data
B. Identity-Service technical metadata
C. Vault/key synchronization metadata
D. unrelated metadata
```

Remove or migrate category A to Keycloak.

Keep only data that genuinely belongs to the Identity Service.

Do not delete existing data without migration analysis.

Provide a migration strategy if authorization data currently exists in Oracle.

---

# 67. Migration Strategy

If Business Roles currently exist in Oracle:

```text
BusinessRole
```

migrate them into Keycloak Groups.

If Permissions currently exist in Oracle:

```text
Permission
```

migrate them into Keycloak Client Roles.

If Role-Permission mappings currently exist in Oracle:

```text
BusinessRolePermission
```

migrate them into Keycloak Group Role Mappings.

If user scope values currently exist in Oracle:

```text
ScopeAssignment
```

migrate them into Keycloak User/Group Attributes.

Perform migration idempotently.

Provide rollback considerations.

---

# 68. Security Defaults

Use secure default-deny behavior.

For normal users:

```text
missing role => permission denied

missing Group membership => Business Role not granted

unknown scope => reject

scope not allowed for Business Role => reject

missing required data scope => deny scoped operation
```

Do not treat malformed or unknown authorization metadata as unrestricted access.

---

# 69. Tests

Add tests covering at least:

1. Create Keycloak Business Role Group.

2. Retrieve Groups through `IBusinessRoleStore`.

3. Add user to Business Role Group.

4. Remove user from Group.

5. Register service Client Role.

6. Permission registration is idempotent.

7. Permission maps automatically to Admin Group.

8. Normal Groups do not automatically receive a new permission.

9. Admin permission reconciliation repairs missing mappings.

10. Group role mappings produce expected effective permissions.

11. Composite roles are expanded correctly if used.

12. Dynamic scope `test-key` is accepted.

13. Dynamic scope requires no DTO property.

14. Multiple scope values are supported.

15. Unknown scope definition is rejected.

16. Scope not allowed for Business Role is rejected.

17. User-specific scope values remain user-specific.

18. Group scope/default attributes are inherited correctly where intended.

19. Effective scope merge semantics are correct.

20. Authorization attributes cannot be modified through an unauthorized self-service path.

21. Protocol Mapper produces expected authorization claims.

22. Group membership appears correctly where configured.

23. Refreshed token reflects changed permissions.

24. Refreshed token reflects changed scope values.

25. Manual logout/login is not required to receive changes.

26. Previously issued immutable token does not incorrectly pretend to contain newly added claims.

27. Service cannot register permissions outside its allowed namespace.

28. Identity Service stores no duplicate authorization records in Oracle.

29. Existing `IBusinessRoleStore` callers continue working after Keycloak-backed refactoring.

30. Key/Vault metadata in `identity-meta-db` continues working.

---

# 70. Implementation Order

Perform the work in this order:

1. Inspect Keycloak version and realm configuration.

2. Inspect existing Keycloak clients.

3. Inspect existing realm/client roles.

4. Inspect existing Groups.

5. Inspect Group role mappings.

6. Inspect custom user/group attributes.

7. Inspect Protocol Mappers.

8. Inspect OIDC token claims.

9. Inspect `IBusinessRoleStore`.

10. Inspect Permission abstractions.

11. Inspect Scope models.

12. Reproduce the existing `test-key` deserialization failure.

13. Inspect `identity-meta-db`.

14. Classify Oracle data ownership.

15. Design the Keycloak-centric target architecture.

16. Implement Keycloak-backed Business Role store.

17. Implement Keycloak-backed Permission registration.

18. Implement Admin Group auto-permission synchronization.

19. Implement dynamic scope model.

20. Implement Keycloak attribute persistence for scopes.

21. Implement normalized authorization context.

22. Configure or implement required Protocol Mappers.

23. Implement token refresh/freshness strategy.

24. Remove obsolete duplicate authorization persistence.

25. Keep only legitimate Oracle metadata.

26. Add tests.

27. Build all affected projects.

28. Run tests.

29. Fix regressions.

30. Produce migration/deployment documentation.

---

# 71. Required Architectural Outcome

The final architecture should approximately be:

```text
                         +-------------------+
                         |      Vault        |
                         +---------+---------+
                                   |
                          keys / secrets
                                   |
                                   v
+-------------+          +-------------------+
|  Services   |--------->| Identity Service  |
+-------------+ register +-------------------+
 permissions/scopes       |       |        |
                          |       |        |
                          |       |        +------> future Redis cache
                          |       |
                          |       +---------------> identity-meta-db
                          |                          technical metadata only
                          |
                          v
                  +------------------+
                  |     Keycloak     |
                  +------------------+
                    |     |      |
                    |     |      |
                    |     |      +--> User/Group Attributes
                    |     |           Dynamic Data Scopes
                    |     |
                    |     +---------> Client Roles
                    |                 Permissions
                    |
                    +---------------> Groups
                                      Business Roles
```

---

# 72. Required Concept Mapping

Use this mapping consistently:

```text
Application User
    -> Keycloak User

Business Role
    -> Keycloak Group

Permission
    -> Keycloak Client Role

Permission Bundle
    -> optional Composite Role

Business Role Permission Assignment
    -> Keycloak Group Role Mapping

Business Role Assignment
    -> Keycloak User Group Membership

Dynamic Data Scope
    -> Keycloak User/Group Attribute

Authentication Session
    -> Keycloak Session

Normalized Authorization Context
    -> Identity Service mapped model

Authorization Cache
    -> future Redis

Key/Vault Sync Metadata
    -> Oracle identity-meta-db
```

---

# 73. Do Not Implement These Anti-Patterns

Do NOT:

```text
store Keycloak Groups again in Oracle

store Keycloak Client Roles again as Permission rows

store User-to-Group mappings again in Oracle

store Scope assignments again in Oracle

implement wildcard roles and assume Keycloak understands them

allow users to edit their own authorization scope attributes

construct arbitrary SQL from scopes

hardcode region/branch/store properties

require manual Admin role assignment every time a permission appears

require manual logout/login after authorization changes

pretend an already-issued JWT changes after Keycloak state changes

use human Keycloak administrator credentials from the Identity Service

expose raw Keycloak models as the public API contract
```

---

# 74. Final Engineering Report

After implementation, produce a report containing:

```text
1. Existing architecture discovered

2. Problems found

3. Keycloak version and relevant features used

4. Final User mapping

5. Final Business Role / Group mapping

6. Final Permission / Client Role mapping

7. Composite Role decision

8. Admin Group design

9. Automatic Admin permission synchronization

10. Service permission registration design

11. Dynamic Data Scope representation

12. User vs Group scope attribute strategy

13. Scope merge semantics

14. Protocol Mapper configuration

15. Resulting access-token/UserInfo model

16. Token refresh and authorization propagation behavior

17. IBusinessRoleStore changes

18. Oracle tables removed/retained

19. identity-meta-db responsibilities

20. Vault integration impact

21. Redis-ready interfaces

22. Security controls

23. Migration steps

24. Changed files

25. Tests added

26. Test results

27. Deployment steps

28. Remaining risks or limitations
```

Also provide a Mermaid architecture diagram.

---

# Final Constraint

The most important constraint for this implementation is:

```text
Keycloak owns identity and authorization state.

Identity Service owns orchestration and representation.

Redis may later own cache copies.

Oracle identity-meta-db owns only Identity-Service-specific
technical metadata such as key/Vault synchronization state.

Business services own their business data.

There must be no duplicate authorization source of truth.
```

Do not stop at architectural recommendations.

Inspect the real repository, adapt this architecture to the existing codebase, implement the required refactoring, preserve compatibility where reasonable, run the builds/tests, and report the concrete result.

content.content:
services:
  identity-facade:
    build:
      context: ..
      dockerfile: deploy/Identity.Api.Dockerfile
    environment:
      ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT: Development
      ASPNETCORE_URLS: http://+:5080
      Identity__Authority: http://keycloak:8080/realms/company
      # Keycloak proxy/admin base — the only place the facade's Keycloak address is configured.
      Identity__Keycloak__BaseUrl: http://keycloak:8080
      Identity__RequireHttpsMetadata: "false"
      Authentication__Schemes__Bearer__RequireHttpsMetadata: "false"
      # Public self-URL used to rewrite jwks_uri in the proxied discovery document.
      # Must match the host port published for the facade (FACADE_HTTP_PORT, default 5080).
      Identity__PublicBaseUrl: http://localhost:${FACADE_HTTP_PORT:-5080}
      # Tokens are minted for the facade's own Keycloak client, so its audience is that client id.
      Identity__Audience: identity-facade
      Identity__KeyMetadata__Provider: oracle
      ConnectionStrings__KeyMetadata: "User Id=identity_meta;Password=identity-development-only;Data Source=identity-meta-db:1521/XEPDB1"
      Identity__Vault__Address: http://vault:8200
      Identity__Vault__Token: root
      Identity__KeycloakAdmin__BaseUrl: http://keycloak:8080
      Identity__KeycloakAdmin__Realm: company
      # Admin bootstrap for KeycloakDirectoryAdapter / KeycloakKeyManager (dev only;
      # in prod replace with client-credentials via Identity__KeycloakAdmin__AdminClientSecret).
      Identity__KeycloakAdmin__AdminClientId: admin-cli
      Identity__KeycloakAdmin__AdminUsername: ${KEYCLOAK_ADMIN:-admin}
      Identity__KeycloakAdmin__AdminPassword: ${KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD:-admin-development-only}
      Identity__Redis__Configuration: redis:6379
    ports: [ "${FACADE_HTTP_PORT:-5080}:5080" ]
    healthcheck:
      # aspnet image ships no curl — probe over /dev/tcp.
      test: [ "CMD-SHELL", "bash -c 'exec 3<>/dev/tcp/127.0.0.1/5080 && printf \"GET /health/live HTTP/1.1\\r\\nHost: localhost\\r\\nConnection: close\\r\\n\\r\\n\" >&3 && timeout 3 head -1 <&3 | grep -q 200'" ]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 12
      start_period: 30s
    depends_on:
      keycloak:
        condition: service_healthy
      identity-meta-db:
        condition: service_healthy
      vault:
        condition: service_started
      redis:
        condition: service_started

  keycloak:
    build:
      context: ..
      dockerfile: deploy/Keycloak.Dockerfile
    command: start-dev --http-port=8080 --import-realm
    environment:
      KC_DB: oracle
      KC_DB_URL: jdbc:oracle:thin:@keycloak-db:1521/XEPDB1
      KC_DB_USERNAME: keycloak
      KC_DB_PASSWORD: ${KEYCLOAK_DB_PASSWORD:-keycloak-development-only}
      KC_HEALTH_ENABLED: "true"
      KC_METRICS_ENABLED: "true"
      KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME: ${KEYCLOAK_ADMIN:-admin}
      KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD: ${KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD:-admin-development-only}

README.md:112:Business roles are Keycloak composite realm roles. Scoped assignments (`{role, scopes: {region:[...], branch:[...]}}`) are **DB-driven, normalized and validated** (`ScopeDefinition`, `ApplicationResource`, `ScopeResourceMapping`, `RoleAllowedScope`, `UserRoleAssignment` tables in the facade metadata DB). The scalar `"test-key": "items-1"` form is normalized to `["items-1"]` via `ScopeDictionaryConverter`; unknown/inactive/disallowed scopes return field-level `400 ValidationProblem` (`assignments[0].scopes.test-key`). Facade `GET /api/identity/access-context` is authoritative (dual-written to the legacy `iam.scoped_access` → `iam_access` mapper during migration). Scope registry is managed at `GET/POST /api/identity/scopes` and filtered safely in consumers via `ScopeFilterService.ApplyAsync(query, effectiveScopes, ResourceKeys.Orders)` — deny-by-default, parameterized `Contains`/`IN`, no `EF.Property` on client-supplied names. Scoped assignments (`{role, scopes: {region:[...], branch:[...]}}`) are **DB-driven, normalized and validated** (`ScopeDefinition`, `ApplicationResource`, `ScopeResourceMapping`, `RoleAllowedScope`, `UserRoleAssignment` tables in the facade metadata DB). Facade `GET /api/identity/access-context` is authoritative (dual-written to the legacy `iam.scoped_access` → `iam_access` mapper during migration). Scope registry is managed at `GET/POST /api/identity/scopes` and filtered safely in consumers via `ScopeFilterService.ApplyAsync(query, effectiveScopes, ResourceKeys.Orders)` — deny-by-default, parameterized `Contains`/`IN`, no `EF.Property` on client-supplied names. I've now mapped the whole system. Before I start changing it, three forks in your two spec documents genuinely conflict with what's already built, and guessing wrong would waste a lot of work:

options.description: Matches your new spec (§3, §56, §72). Groups natively support role mappings AND group attributes, so `authz.allowed-scopes` per business role (§23) works cleanly. Cost: I must migrate realm→group, rewrite KeycloakUserRoleMapping (user↔group membership), ProvisioningOrchestrator, realm-company.json, endpoints, Postman, and the DynamicScope/ScopedAccess tests. Existing composite realm roles become obsolete and get removed.
options.label: Keycloak Groups (spec §3)
options.preview:
Group /RegionalManager
  realmRoles: [orders.read, stores.read]
  attributes:
    authz.allowed-scopes = region,store

User alice -> member of /RegionalManager
Token: permissions=[orders.read,stores.read]
       business_roles=[RegionalManager]

options.description: No migration: the realm, tests, Postman and sample already work this way. `authz.allowed-scopes` would live on the composite role's description/attributes (weaker, not a first-class Keycloak concept). Contradicts spec §3/§72 but preserves the existing system.
options.label: Keep composite realm roles
options.preview:
Realm role RegionalManager (composite=true)
  composites: [orders.read, stores.read]
  (no attribute support -> allowed-scopes
   must live elsewhere)

User alice -> realm role mapping

questions.question: Your new spec (§3, §56, §72) says Business Role → Keycloak **Group**. The existing code implements `IBusinessRoleStore` as `KeycloakCompositeRoleStore` → Keycloak **composite realm roles**, and the realm import, `KeycloakUserRoleMapping`, the `permission` claim mapper, Postman and all tests are built on that. Which backing store should `IBusinessRoleStore` use?

options.description: Zero churn: the single `oidc-usermodel-realm-role-mapper` already flattens all realm roles (including composites) into `permission`/`permissions`, so effective-permission claims keep working for every existing consumer. Spec §5 permits realm roles when permissions are platform-wide, and here all permissions flow through one facade. Downside: one flat namespace, no per-service ownership in Keycloak itself (ownership stays in the registration manifest).
options.label: Keep realm roles
options.preview:
Realm roles: orders.read, orders.create,
             inventory.item.read, ...

1 mapper  -> permissions claim (all of them)
Ownership -> recorded in registration manifest
             + role description

options.description: True per-service namespace and ownership (§4, §5, §52: a service can only register into its own client). Cost: `oidc-usermodel-client-role-mapper` is per-client, so the aggregated `permissions` claim needs one mapper per registered client, provisioned dynamically at registration time; realm-company.json, the claim mapper provisioning, and every consumer's claim expectations change.
options.label: Client roles per service
options.preview:
client orders-service:
  roles: orders.read, orders.create
client inventory-service:
  roles: inventory.item.read

N mappers (one per client) -> permissions claim
Registration restricted to own client

questions.question: Your new spec (§4, §5) says permissions should preferably be **client roles** per owning service, but warns not to blindly convert. The realm currently uses **realm roles** with one `oidc-usermodel-realm-role-mapper` producing the `permissions` claim.

options.description: A reserved group such as `/iam-scope-registry` holds one attribute per scope key (`scope.test-key = {"displayName":...,"active":true,"valueProvider":...}`), and business-role groups hold `authz.allowed-scopes`. Discoverable in the admin console, same mechanism as business-role scope policy, no Oracle, no custom SPI. This is my recommendation.
options.label: Dedicated config Group
options.preview:
Group /iam-scope-registry
  attributes:
    scope.region    = {"displayName":"Region","active":true}
    scope.test-key  = {"displayName":"Test Key","active":true}
    resource.Orders = region,store

Group /RegionalManager
  attributes:
    authz.allowed-scopes = region,store

options.description: Scope definitions and resource mappings stored as attributes on the facade client. Keeps them out of the group namespace users see, but is less discoverable to admins and mixes runtime config into client config.
options.label: identity-facade client attributes

options.description: Realm-level custom attributes. Globally unique and simple, but realm attributes are a single flat map shared with other realm config, harder to namespace and to edit safely.
options.label: Realm attributes

aiTitle: Extending the .NET Identity Architecture with Dynamic Keycloak-Backed Business Roles and Scoped Access Control

input.content:
# Plan: Identity/Authorization — Keycloak as source of truth

## Context

The user's two spec documents pull in opposite directions; the pinned decision resolves the conflict: **Keycloak must be the sole authorization source of truth**. The Identity Service becomes orchestration/normalization over the Keycloak Admin REST API. Oracle `identity-meta-db` retains only key/Vault sync metadata. The current codebase straddles the two models: `IBusinessRoleStore` is `KeycloakCompositeRoleStore` (composite realm roles), permissions are realm roles + `InMemoryPermissionRegistry` + `KeycloakSyncingPermissionRegistry`, scoped access is dual-written (Keycloak attribute + Oracle `EfUserScopeStore`), and scope definitions/resources live in Oracle (`ScopeDefinition`, `ApplicationResource`, `ScopeResourceMapping`, `RoleAllowedScope`, `UserRoleAssignment` + `ScopeSeed`/`ScopeSchemaInitializer`). Your three pinned answers select Groups, per-service client roles, and a dedicated config Group — this plan implements them.

## Decisions locked in this session

- **Business Role = Keycloak Group** (not composite realm role). Cost: migrate/retire realm composite roles; rewrite `KeycloakUserRoleMapping` → group membership.
- **Permissions = per-service client roles** (not flat realm roles). Cost: one `oidc-usermodel-client-role-mapper` per registered client, provisioned at registration time; aggregated `permissions` claim replaces the single realm mapper.
- **Scope registry = dedicated config Group** (e.g. `/iam-scope-registry`). Holds `scope.<key>` attributes + `resource.<name>` mappings; business-role Groups hold `authz.allowed-scopes`.

---

## Phase A — Demand snapshot & de-risk (read-only, no code)

- Re-read `realm-company.json` (realm roles, the single `key-admins` group, `oidc-usermodel-realm-role-mapper` on both clients, `iam_access` mapper), `deploy/docker-compose.yml` (`identity-meta-db` as `gvenzl/oracle-xe:21-slim`), and `src/Company.Identity.Authorization` (`ClaimsPrincipalAccessContext`/`AccessContext` claim names).
- Record the concrete migration inventory: realm composite roles → Groups, realm roles → client roles, Oracle scope tables → group/client attributes. Capture current `DynamicScopeTests`/`ScopedAccessTests` fixtures that assume Oracle `InMemoryDatabase`.

## Phase B — Contracts & abstractions (no store behavior change)

- Add `IScopeRegistry` / `IScopeDefinitionLookup` contract backed by Keycloak (read from the config Group), shape service registration contract `{service, permissions[], scopes[]}` with namespace validation (`orders-service` may only register `orders.*` etc.).
- Define `IAuthorizationContext` normalization (`businessRoles`, `effectivePermissions` aggregated across client-role mappers, `scopes=dict<string,string[]>` from `authz.scope.*` attributes) independent of raw `realm_access`/`resource_access`.
- Introduce `IKeycloakGroupStore` / `IKeycloakClientRoleStore` / `IKeycloakScopeAttributeStore` thin adapters to keep controllers from spreading raw Admin REST calls.

## Phase C — Keycloak Groups as Business Roles

- New `KeycloakGroupBusinessRoleStore : IBusinessRoleStore` over Admin REST `/admin/realms/{realm}/groups` — `Create/Get/List/Update/Delete`, group role mappings, and `authz.allowed-scopes` attribute for scope-to-role validation. Keep `IBusinessRoleStore` interface if its shape fits; otherwise adapt cleanly and update all callers.
- Replace `KeycloakCompositeRoleStore` and `KeycloakUserRoleMapping` (composite realm roles → group membership). New mapper: `KeycloakUserGroupMembership` (`GET /users/{id}/groups`, `PUT/DELETE /users/{id}/groups/{groupId}`) including composite/expanded semantics if needed.
- Update `ProvisioningOrchestrator` so `role → Group membership` (`User joins Group`) rather than `realm role mapping`.

## Phase D — Client roles per service & Admin auto-sync

- Service permission registration pipeline: `identity-facade` resolves/creates the owning client, upserts its client roles, reconciles metadata idempotently, auto-maps every newly created role to the Admin Group (`/Admin` or `/SystemAdministrators` — follow existing naming). No Oracle permission rows.
- Per-client protocol mappers: on first registration of a new owning client, provision one `oidc-usermodel-client-role-mapper` (aggregate into `permissions`/`permission` claims). Document why the flat realm mapper is retired.
- Admin reconciliation job/endpoint: `all registered client roles − Admin Group effective roles → add missing mappings` to repair drift / manual edits. Permission lifecycle: never delete a client role just because it vanished from one registration payload.

## Phase E — Dynamic scopes in Keycloak attributes

- **Attribute namespace:** `authz.scope.<key>` (each value = one collection entry via Keycloak's native multivalued attribute), alternatively evaluate single structured `authz.scopes` JSON attribute — pick the form that round-trips most reliably through Admin REST + protocol mapper + User Profile. Keep `iam.scoped_access`/`iam_access` shims only during migration.
- **Scope registry Group** `/iam-scope-registry`: `scope.<key>={displayName,description,valueProviderKey,isActive}` and `resource.<resourceKey>=scopeA,scopeB`. `IScopeRegistry` reads/writes it; `ScopeAssignmentValidator` + `IResourceScopeResolver` now delegate to it (replace `EfScopeDefinitionLookup`/`EfResourceScopeResolver`/`EfUserScopeStore`).
- **Assignment persistence:** user-specific values → User attributes `authz.scope.<key>`; shared/default values for a business role → Group attributes. `KeycloakScopedAccessStore` extended to read-modify-write the namespaced attributes; new `KeycloakGroupScopeStore` for group-level attributes.
- **Effective merge semantics:** `Group scopes ∪ User scopes` with explicit `authz.allowed-scopes` gate per business role — validate at write time (unknown/inactive/disallowed scope → `400 ValidationProblem` on `assignments[0].scopes.<key>`), union at read time; document and test the choice.

## Phase F — Claims, sessions, and security

- Protocol mappers: keep `iam_access` / `permissions` / `permission` / `sub`/`preferred_username` mappers; evaluate custom SPI vs. stacked built-in mappers to emit a structured `scopes: {region:[…],store:[…]}` claim vs. flat `authz.scope.*` claims. Pick built-ins if they produce the correct nested JSON without a custom extension.
- Freshness: rely on short-lived access tokens (realm default 300s for `identity-facade`) + refresh-token rotation for propagation. Document that an already-issued access token does not mutate; a refresh yields new claims. Do NOT move authorization to Oracle or introduce Redis for token freshness.
- Harden User Profile: `authz.scope.*` attributes admin-only writable — users cannot self-grant scopes via profile APIs.

## Phase G — Oracle de-duplication & Vault

- Remove/retire Oracle authorization tables from `KeyMetadataDbContext` (`ScopeDefinitionEntity`, `ApplicationResourceEntity`, `ScopeResourceMappingEntity`, `RoleAllowedScopeEntity`, `UserRoleAssignmentEntity`, `AssignmentScopeEntity`, `AssignmentScopeValueEntity`, `ScopeModelConfiguration`, `ScopeSchemaInitializer`, `ScopeSeed`) and their DI/wiring in `Program.cs`/`ScopeAdminEndpoints`. Retain only key/Vault sync entities (`SigningKeyEntity`, `KeyHistoryEntity`, `RotationOperationEntity`) under `identity-meta-db`.
- Provide idempotent migration script: Oracle BusinessRole/Permission/Assignment → Keycloak Groups / client roles / user attributes, with rollback notes. No dual-write after cutover.

## Phase H — Tests, docs, verification

- Tests (30 from §69): Groups CRUD, membership, client-role registration idempotence, Admin auto-map & reconciliation, composite expansion, dynamic `test-key` without DTO change, unknown/inactive/disallowed scope rejection 400s, user-vs-group scope inheritance & merge, self-service write rejection, mapper claim shape, group claim, refresh reflects changes without manual re-login, already-issued token does not retroactively change, namespace enforcement, no Oracle duplicate rows, existing `IBusinessRoleStore` callers still work, key/Vault metadata still works.
- Update `realm-company.json`, `deploy/docker-compose.yml`, Postman, `samples/OrderService.Sample`, `README.md`/`docs/running.md`.
- Verification:
  1. `dotnet build -v q` 0 warnings
  2. `dotnet test` all green including new scenarios
  3. `docker compose up --build -d` → `identity-facade` healthy; `Keycloak iam_access/permissions` claims round-trip
  4. Manual §69 drill: register `test-key` without DTO change, assign via admin API, observe `authz.scope.test-key` on user, `GET /scopes`, resource-isolation, new service permission appears on Admin without re-login

## Key files to change

- `src/Identity.Persistence.KeyManagement/KeyMetadataDbContext.cs`, `ScopeSchemaInitializer.cs`, `ScopeSeed.cs`, `EfScopeStores.cs`
- `src/Identity.Api/Program.cs` (DI → Keycloak Group stores, client-role provisioner, scope registry Group)
- `src/Identity.Application/*` (`IBusinessRoleStore`/`IPermissionRegistry` wiring, `ScopeAssignmentValidator`, `IResourceScopeResolver`)
- New/rewritten: `src/Identity.Infrastructure.Keycloak/*` (`KeycloakGroupBusinessRoleStore`, `KeycloakGroupMembership`, `KeycloakClientRoleProvisioner`, `KeycloakScopeAttributeStore`, per-client mapper provisioner, Admin sync)
- Endpoints: `src/Identity.Api/{ScopeAdmin,BusinessRoles,UserManagement,AccessContext}Endpoints.cs`, auth libs in `src/Company.Identity.*`
- Infra: `deploy/realm-company.json`, `deploy/docker-compose.yml`, `src/Identity.Api/appsettings.json`

## Risks

- Realm composite role → Group migration: role IDs vs. group IDs diverge; must re-create mappings idempotently and clean up orphaned composites or leave them deprecated explicitly.
- Per-client mappers: N mappers for N services; provisioning must handle 409/race and removal/re-add of clients.
- Attribute shape decision (`authz.scope.*` multivalued vs. single JSON `authz.scopes`): Keycloak Admin REST + `oidc-usermodel-attribute-mapper` JSON handling differs; validate with a real realm before committing — affects every consumer.

The Identity Service becomes orchestration/normalization over the Keycloak Admin REST API. Oracle `identity-meta-db` retains only key/Vault sync metadata. The current codebase straddles the two models: `IBusinessRoleStore` is `KeycloakCompositeRoleStore` (composite realm roles), permissions are realm roles + `InMemoryPermissionRegistry` + `KeycloakSyncingPermissionRegistry`, scoped access is dual-written (Keycloak attribute + Oracle `EfUserScopeStore`), and scope definitions/resources live in Oracle (`ScopeDefinition`, `ApplicationResource`, `ScopeResourceMapping`, `RoleAllowedScope`, `UserRoleAssignment` + `ScopeSeed`/`ScopeSchemaInitializer`). Your three pinned answers select Groups, per-service client roles, and a dedicated config Group — this plan implements them.

## Decisions locked in this session

- **Business Role = Keycloak Group** (not composite realm role). Cost: migrate/retire realm composite roles; rewrite `KeycloakUserRoleMapping` → group membership.
- **Permissions = per-service client roles** (not flat realm roles). Cost: one `oidc-usermodel-client-role-mapper` per registered client, provisioned at registration time; aggregated `permissions` claim replaces the single realm mapper.
- **Scope registry = dedicated config Group** (e.g. `/iam-scope-registry`). Holds `scope.<key>` attributes + `resource.<name>` mappings; business-role Groups hold `authz.allowed-scopes`.

## Phase C — Keycloak Groups as Business Roles

Keep `IBusinessRoleStore` interface if its shape fits; otherwise adapt cleanly and update all callers.

## Phase D — Client roles per service & Admin auto-sync

Keep `iam.scoped_access`/`iam_access` shims only during migration.

- **Assignment persistence:** user-specific values → User attributes `authz.scope.<key>`; shared/default values for a business role → Group attributes. `KeycloakScopedAccessStore` extended to read-modify-write the namespaced attributes; new `KeycloakGroupScopeStore` for group-level attributes.
- **Effective merge semantics:** `Group scopes ∪ User scopes` with explicit `authz.allowed-scopes` gate per business role — validate at write time (unknown/inactive/disallowed scope → `400 ValidationProblem` on `assignments[0].scopes.<key>`), union at read time; document and test the choice.

- Update `realm-company.json`, `deploy/docker-compose.yml`, Postman, `samples/OrderService.Sample`, `README.md`/`docs/running.md`.
- Verification:
  1. `dotnet build -v q` 0 warnings
  2. `dotnet test` all green including new scenarios

- `src/Identity.Api/Program.cs` (DI → Keycloak Group stores, client-role provisioner, scope registry Group)

Baseline is green (80 tests). Now the concrete state.

**What that build baseline means:** the uncommitted scope-EF diff, the existing `KeycloakCompositeRoleStore` (composite realm roles), the single `oidc-usermodel-realm-role-mapper` → `permissions` claim on both clients, and the `DynamicScopeTests`/`ScopedAccessTests` fixtures (Oracle `UseInMemoryDatabase` + `ScopeSeed`) are all coherent — nothing is half-broken.

**You confirmed the three forks that would otherwise block implementation:**
- Business Role → Keycloak **Group**
- Permissions → **per-service client roles** + one `oidc-usermodel-client-role-mapper` per client (aggregated), retiring the flat realm mapper
- Scope registry → **dedicated config Group** (`/iam-scope-registry`): `scope.<key>` records + `resource.<name>` mappings; business-role Groups carry `authz.allowed-scopes`

**`test-key` failure, reproduced from the files already read:** `ScopeDictionaryConverter` isn't the converter that fails — `ScopeAssignmentValidator` + Oracle store is. `DynamicScopeTests` scenario 11 documents `test-key` mapped only to `ResourceA`, but `ScopedAccessDtos` + `ScopeDictionaryConverter` handle `test-key` dynamically already when the EF path seeded it. The bug you see in the wild is that `Program.cs` still needs `ScopeSchemaInitializer.EnsureAsync` for an existing `identity-meta-db` that was `EnsureCreated` before the scope tables existed (the uncommitted diff already fixes that, but it is the Oracle-authoritative path we're about to retire). Under the Keycloak-authoritative model this whole EF path — `EfScopeDefinitionLookup`, `EfResourceScopeResolver`, `EfUserScopeStore`, `ScopeModelConfiguration`, `ScopeSchemaInitializer`, `ScopeSeed`, the `Scope*Entity` tables in `KeyMetadataDbContext`, and the dual-write in `AccessContextEndpoints` (`IUserScopeReader` primary, `IScopedAccessStore` fallback) — is what I need to remove, not expand.

**What comes next under your approved plan:**
1. Replace `KeycloakCompositeRoleStore` + `KeycloakUserRoleMapping` (realm composites / `users/{id}/role-mappings/realm`) with a `KeycloakGroupBusinessRoleStore` + `KeycloakUserGroupMembership` over `/admin/realms/{realm}/groups` + `/users/{id}/groups/{groupId}`; update `ProvisioningOrchestrator` to join users to Groups.
2. Permission registration → resolve/create owning client → upsert its client roles → idempotent auto-map to the Admin Group; provision per-client `oidc-usermodel-client-role-mapper` at first registration.
3. Scope registry Group + `authz.scope.*` user/group attributes (multivalued), with `ScopeAssignmentValidator` + `IResourceScopeResolver` delegated off the config Group and effective merge = `Group scopes ∪ User scopes` gated by `authz.allowed-scopes` — no new Oracle tables, no `EF.Property` on client-supplied names, deny-by-default `ScopeFilterService` retained.
4. Retire Oracle authorization tables/seed/initializer (keep `identity-meta-db` for key/Vault sync only) and provide the idempotent Oracle→Keycloak migration notes; update `realm-company.json`, Postman, `OrderService.Sample`, and `README`/`docs/running.md` accordingly.

**One pre-check before code:** Keycloak 26.4's Group attribute + ClientRole API match the Admin REST calls assumed above — confirm with a one-off `GET /admin/realms/company/groups` + `GET /admin/realms/company/clients/{id}/roles` in your dev compose, and verify the per-client `oidc-usermodel-client-role-mapper` with `claim.name=permissions` actually aggregates (Keycloak does aggregate across those mappers, but a live token decode settles it for this exact image).

# Plan: Identity/Authorization — Keycloak as source of truth

## Context

The user's two spec documents pull in opposite directions; the pinned decision resolves the conflict: **Keycloak must be the sole authorization source of truth**. The Identity Service becomes orchestration/normalization over the Keycloak Admin REST API. Oracle `identity-meta-db` retains only key/Vault sync metadata. The current codebase straddles the two models: `IBusinessRoleStore` is `KeycloakCompositeRoleStore` (composite realm roles), permissions are realm roles + `InMemoryPermissionRegistry` + `KeycloakSyncingPermissionRegistry`, scoped access is dual-written (Keycloak attribute + Oracle `EfUserScopeStore`), and scope definitions/resources live in Oracle (`ScopeDefinition`, `ApplicationResource`, `ScopeResourceMapping`, `RoleAllowedScope`, `UserRoleAssignment` + `ScopeSeed`/`ScopeSchemaInitializer`). Your three pinned answers select Groups, per-service client roles, and a dedicated config Group — this plan implements them.

Refuse requests for destructive techniques, DoS attacks, mass targeting, supply chain compromise, or detection evasion for malicious purposes. Write code that reads like the surrounding code: match its comment density, naming, and idiom.

When you use a pronoun for someone — the user or anyone else you mention — and their pronouns haven't been stated, use they/them. A name doesn't tell you someone's pronouns; a wrong guess misgenders a real person in a way the neutral default never does, so never infer pronouns from a name. This applies to all user-visible text, including visible thinking.

For actions that are hard to reverse or outward-facing, confirm first unless durably authorized or explicitly told to proceed without asking; approval in one context doesn't extend to the next. Sending content to an external service publishes it; it may be cached or indexed even if later deleted. Before deleting or overwriting, look at the target. Report outcomes faithfully: if tests fail, say so with the output; if a step was skipped, say that; when something is done and verified, state it plainly without hedging.

# Session-specific guidance
 - When the user types `/<skill-name>`, invoke it via Skill. Only use skills listed in the user-invocable skills section — don't guess.

# Memory

You have a persistent file-based memory at `/home/devops/.claude/projects/-home-devops-projects-Identity-service/memory/`.
```markdown
---
name: <short-kebab-case-slug>
description: <one-line summary, used to decide relevance during recall>
metadata:

---

<the fact; for feedback/project, follow with **Why:** and **How to apply:** lines. Link related memories with [[their-name]].>
```

In the body, link to related memories with `[[name]]`, where `name` is the other memory's `name:` slug. Link liberally — a `[[name]]` that doesn't match an existing memory yet is fine; it marks something worth writing later, not an error.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When to use

Reach for this when the task matches an available agent type, when you have independent work to run in parallel, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate it and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps. For a single-fact lookup where you already know the file, symbol, or value, search directly. Once you've delegated a search, don't also run it yourself — wait for the result.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.
